Affiliation: The University of Sydney Abstract A common assumption in chain-of-thought (CoT) oversight is that a visible reasoning trace makes model behavior easier to monitor. We argue that this assumption can conflate distinct properties along a chain linking a model’s internal computation, reasoning artifacts, outputs, and monitor judgments. We identify four properties along this chain: reasoning visibility (whether a trace is accessible), mechanistic faithfulness (whether a trace reflects internal computation), mechanistic localizability (whether a compact causal mechanism can be isolated), and behavioral monitorability (whether a monitor can detect the target behavior). Two complementary case studies across three open-weight reasoning models show why these distinctions matter. In the security vulnerability reasoning study, probes and activation ablations provide evidence of internal representation and causal influence, but a monitor with access to the reference answer does not outperform the majority-class baseline in a held-out test. In the authority-hint factual reasoning study, a monitor correctly distinguishes changed from unchanged answers, but seven mechanistic analyses do not isolate a compact causal mechanism. These results show that evidence for one claim does not establish the others. We therefore propose an evidential-chain reporting standard. Each claim carries a licensing statement that specifies its target property, access tier, and artifact, and labels each required link as supported, unsupported, or assumed. These assessments determine whether the conclusion is licensed, conditionally licensed, or not licensed. 1 Introduction Reasoning artifacts are increasingly used to oversee large language models (LLMs). By exposing intermediate judgments, assumptions, and reasoning steps, chain-of-thought (CoT) traces may help human experts or automated monitors evaluate more than the final answer [ 19 , 4 ] . A common assumption is that a visible trace therefore makes model behavior easier to monitor [ 27 , 9 , 17 ] . This leaves two separate questions. Does the trace reflect the computation behind the answer? And can a monitor use what it is given to identify the target property? These concern mechanistic faithfulness and behavioral monitorability , respectively. Prior work has shown that reasoning can be visible without being faithful , e.g., a plausible trace may omit or misrepresent factors that drove the model’s answer [ 35 , 9 , 5 ] . Such omissions can limit monitoring when decisive information is unavailable [ 37 ] . Even when relevant information is available, a monitor may fail to evaluate it correctly. Faithfulness studies examine whether stated reasoning reflects the factors driving model behavior [ 18 , 23 ] , while monitorability studies evaluate whether external monitors can detect errors, reward hacking, or other target behaviors [ 4 , 12 , 25 ] . Mechanistic interpretability investigates internal features and causal pathways [ 34 , 20 ] . These approaches answer different questions. Using evidence for one property to support a claim about another therefore needs justification. Faithfulness evaluations have been discussed as proxies for monitorability [ 17 , 25 ] . Other work treats faithful information flow through the CoT as necessary for monitoring [ 16 ] . In this work, we place four properties along a chain from model to monitor [ 2 , 16 ] . The chain runs from the model’s internal computation (its activations and the causal pathways through them), through what it produces (the reasoning trace and the final output), to a monitor’s verdict on a target property. Mechanistic localizability is about the computation itself. Mechanistic faithfulness is about the link from computation to trace. Reasoning visibility is about whether the trace is disclosed. Behavioral monitorability is about the link from trace and output to the verdict (Section 2.2 ). Position: Evidence for mechanistic faithfulness does not, by itself, establish behavioral monitorability, nor vice versa. CoT oversight claims must declare their target property and distinguish tested links from assumed ones. Through two complementary case studies, we illustrate that supporting one link in this chain does not establish the others. In the security vulnerability case (Section 3 ), linear probes recover key reasoning-step content from internal activations, and interventions on a decoded direction affect model outputs. These findings provide evidence of representation and causal influence, not a full validation of trace faithfulness. Yet an LLM jury, given the original code, reasoning trace, final answer, and reference answer, does not outperform the majority-class baseline on classification in a held-out test. For example, a model claimed that embedded null characters caused a buffer overflow. The jury unanimously accepted the analysis, but human review rejected it as technically incorrect (Section 3 ). In authority-hint factual reasoning (Section 4 ), an external monitor correctly distinguishes changed from unchanged answers on a small balanced set of cases. A rule that looks only at the final answer does equally well, so this evaluation does not establish an additional contribution from the reasoning trace. Seven mechanistic analyses, however, fail to isolate a compact causal mechanism for the behavior. The monitor succeeds on these cases, but the trace’s faithfulness remains unverified. Failure to isolate a compact causal mechanism does not show that no such mechanism exists or that the traces are unfaithful. The paper makes three contributions. First, we distinguish four oversight properties and connect each to its evidential requirements. Second, we provide two case studies that compare internal representation, behavioral monitoring, and compact localization, and we replicate the security-monitor conclusion on QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-70B. Third, to make these distinctions explicit, we propose an evidential chain standard for reporting oversight claims: each claim is reported with a licensing statement 1 1 1 Licensing is used in its evidential rather than its legal sense: a statement specifies which uses of the evidence are warranted. that specifies its target property, the reasoning access tier and artifact examined, and the evidential chain behind it. For each required link, the statement records whether it is supported, unsupported, or assumed, and a conclusion is licensed accordingly (Section 5 ). 2 From Reasoning Disclosure to Oversight Properties A common source of confusion in CoT oversight is that different papers observe different reasoning artifacts (internal activations, raw traces, provider-summarized traces, user-facing explanations) and draw conclusions as if they were interchangeable. They are not. We first distinguish the artifacts available for CoT oversight, then define the properties that require separate evidence. 2.1 Reasoning access tiers What a monitor can conclude depends on what it can see. We distinguish four access tiers , ordered by proximity to the model’s computation: • Tier I: Internal computation. Hidden activations, features, residual streams, attention patterns, and causal pathways, as used in probing, activation patching, or circuit analysis. • Tier II: Raw reasoning trace. Directly available generated reasoning tokens before the final answer, such as <think>...</think> blocks, raw CoT continuations, or scratchpad tokens. • Tier III: Processed reasoning trace. A summarized, filtered, or compressed version of the trace released in its place, such as a provider’s thinking summary. • Tier IV: User-facing explanation. The final explanation presented in an interface or report. Each step from Tier I toward Tier IV can lose information a monitor needs, or add distortions. A provider that summarizes a raw trace (Tier II → \rightarrow III) may remove hedging, backtracking, or self-correction that a monitor would need to assess confidence, while also adding distortions such as overstated coherence or unsupported claims. A user-facing explanation (Tier III → \rightarrow IV) may further optimize for clarity, policy compliance, or persuasion rather than fidelity to the reasoning process. Our empirical claims concern only Tiers I and II, where we have direct access to internal activations and open-weight models. Broader implications for provider disclosure concern the gaps between Tiers II–IV, which we leave to future work. 2.2 Four oversight properties Access tiers specify what is observed; oversight properties specify what is claimed. Even at the same access tier, different oversight questions require different evidence, and evidence at one tier need not transfer to another. We distinguish four properties, each with its own success criterion and failure mode (Table 1 ). Each claim should therefore report both the access tier and the target property. Reasoning visibility. A system has reasoning visibility when some reasoning artifact is available to an observer. Visibility is therefore a disclosure property rather than an accuracy or safety property. It tells you that something is exposed, not that the exposed content is accurate, complete, or useful for oversight. Most current discussions of CoT transparency focus on this level. Mechanistic faithfulness. A reasoning step is mechanistically faithful when its content reflects the internal computation that produces the model’s output. Faithfulness is thus a relation between trace and computation rather than a property of the trace alone. It requires both that activations encode the step’s content and that this encoding causally contributes to the output [ 38 ] . Behavioral monitorability. A behavior is monitorable, for a given class of monitors, when such a monitor detects the target property from the trace or response more accurately than a baseline on held-out cases. Monitorability therefore depends on the monitor. Mechanistic localizability. A behavior is mechanistically localizable when a mechanistic method can identify a compact feature, direction, site, or subcomponent such that intervening on it changes the behavior predictably. Localizability is a stronger requirement than internal representation and can fail even when a computation is real but distributed. Table 1: Oversight properties distinguished in this paper. Each property asks a different question, relies on a different evidence type, and fails for a different reason. Property Core question Evidence type Typical failure mode Reasoning visibility Is reasoning exposed? Trace availability Relevant reasoning exists but is hidden or compressed Mechanistic faithfulness Does the trace reflect internal computation? Representation probes; causal tests when available Trace is unsupported, incomplete, or post-hoc Behavioral monitorability Can a monitor detect the target property? Held-out monitor accuracy vs. baseline Relevant information is present but too hard for the monitor Mechanistic localizability Can a compact mechanism be isolated? Direction finding, site patching, circuit tests Computation is distributed or method-insensitive 2.3 Relation to existing decompositions Existing work draws some of these lines. Barez et al. [ 5 ] separate visible reasoning from explanation, which in our terms is the gap between visibility and faithfulness. Emmons et al. [ 11 ] distinguish CoT-as-rationalization from CoT-as-computation and argue that for runtime monitoring the key property is monitorability rather than faithfulness. Korbak et al. [ 17 ] describe faithfulness evaluations as proxy measures for monitorability, and Meek et al. [ 25 ] combine faithfulness and verbosity into a monitorability score. Guan et al. [ 12 ] measure monitors directly, and Yang et al. [ 37 ] separate verbalization quality from monitor reliability. Anwar et al. [ 2 ] show that target-relevant information in a CoT is necessary but not sufficient for monitoring, and decompose monitor error into an information gap and an elicitation error. Jia et al. [ 16 , 22 ] treat stronger information flow through the CoT as a route to both faithful and monitorable reasoning. Our decomposition differs in treating mechanistic localizability as a separate property and in pairing each property with its own evidence type (Table 1 ). Our position is that these distinctions should become reporting requirements: authors should identify the links each claim requires, state the evidence supporting them, and make unresolved assumptions explicit. The two studies test the inference in both directions: in Section 3 , causal evidence relevant to faithfulness is present but a monitor with full task information fails; in Section 4 , a monitor succeeds but faithfulness is unverified. Table 2 summarizes the corresponding access tiers, target properties, evidence types, and splits. Table 2 : Setup and evidence for the two empirical studies. Access tiers follow Section 2 : Tier I denotes internal activations/mechanisms and Tier II denotes raw generated reasoning traces. Additional implementation and computation details are provided in Appendix A Domain Task Access / property Evidence type Split Security vulnerability reasoning Reasoning-step internal representation Tier I + Tier II/III; internal representation / mechanistic faithfulness Linear probes on activations recorded while the model re-reads its own reasoning. All 200 outputs; 50 correctly solved rows for confirmation Security vulnerability reasoning Held-out monitorability Tier II + task/reference context; behavioral monitorability Structured LLM jury that also sees the reference answer. 30 dev / 59 held-out expert-adjudicated cases Authority-hint factual reasoning Effect of hints on answers Tier II + output behavior; behavioral effect Clean and hinted MMLU/GPQA variants. 1,592 primary rows; strict 48-question replication subset Authority-hint factual reasoning Authority monitorability Tier II; behavioral monitorability Authority-cue monitor decisions. Strict authority cases Authority-hint factual reasoning Mechanistic localization Tier I; mechanistic localizability Control, residual-direction, token × \times layer, and patching tests. Strict mechanistic candidate set Authority-hint factual reasoning Verbalization and restoration Tier I + Tier II; verbalization vs. mechanistic signal Authority-verbalization labels correlated with restoration signal. 32 processed cases; n = 30 n=30 after excluding ambiguous labels 3 Monitor Failure Need Not Indicate Unfaithful Reasoning Using security vulnerability reasoning, we first test whether a monitor’s failure can be read as evidence that a trace is unfaithful. This domain is a useful stress test for CoT oversight because a monitor must distinguish genuinely established vulnerabilities from plausible but unsupported security narratives. Task and model setup. The primary model is DeepSeek-14B. We use QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-70B for held-out monitor replication [ 10 , 33 , 29 ] . The security vulnerability dataset contains 200 CyberSecEval/PurpleLlama-style code-analysis tasks [ 8 , 7 ] , spanning injection, memory safety, and use-after-free. Each task asks whether a vulnerability exists, what type it is, and whether it is reachable or exploitable. 3.1 Testing internal support for reasoning-step content Method and protocol. We test whether the model’s stated security reasoning is recoverable from its internal activations . The analysis uses all 200 outputs. For each example, we feed the original prompt and the model’s own earlier reasoning back through the model as fixed input, rather than generating a new response. We take the hidden states over the first 256 reasoning tokens and average them, per layer, into one activation vector. We then train diagnostic probes on these activations. This follows the standard probing: hidden representations from a fixed model are used as features for lightweight classifiers to test whether a semantic property is recoverable [ 3 , 1 , 6 ] . We evaluate three step-level labels: identifies_vulnerability , traces_data_flow , and assesses_exploitability . Each label records whether the step is present in the trace, not whether it is correct, and is assigned by deterministic rules over the complete normalized reasoning text (Appendix A.2 ); probes are class-weighted logistic regressions with five-fold stratified cross-validation over the layer sweep. For each reasoning step, we select the best layer by mean cross-validated AUC. Recoverability versus faithfulness. The probe results (Figure 1 a) show that the presence of key security-reasoning steps is recoverable from internal activations, with mean cross-validated AUCs between 0.84 and 0.98 (Figure 1 a). However, recoverability is insufficient to separate computation from reading as the trace is part of the model’s input. Text-based classifiers evaluated on the same reasoning spans and folds perform comparably, and the 95% confidence intervals for paired AUC differences between the activation probes and text-based classifiers all include zero. The probes also show no greater advantage over text-based classifiers when processing the model’s own reasoning than when processing analyses by DeepSeek-70B. These results illustrate that reasoning content is recoverable, not that the disclosed reasoning reflects the computation that produces the answer. Causal evidence for faithfulness. To go beyond recoverability, we test whether intervening on the probe direction affects generation. We refitted the vulnerability-identification probe at its best layer on the cases outside the intervention set (Appendix A.2 ). During both prompt processing and generation, we replaced the activation component along the probe direction with its mean over the fitting cases. Five random directions served as controls (Figure 1 b). Two runs without intervention produced identical texts on every case, supporting attribution of the observed changes to the intervention rather than run-to-run variation. Ablation changes the verdict on 15 of 59 cases, against 5–11 for each random direction, and removes identification content in 13 of the 27 cases where it appeared at baseline ( p = 0.051 p=0.051 and 0.034 0.034 ; Figure 1 b). The decoded direction is therefore associated with the stated reasoning step, and intervening on it can change the answer, which is causal evidence relevant to faithfulness. 3.2 Testing monitorability with complete task information A structured jury with the reference answer. To test monitorability, we use a structured LLM jury that also sees the reference answer (a reference-assisted jury). Each juror sees the original code, the model’s reasoning trace, the model’s final answer, and the reference answer. The juror then predicts structured fields for vulnerability existence, vulnerability type, and exploitability. Field-level judgments are aggregated by majority vote and mapped deterministically to an overall label: CORRECT , PARTIALLY_CORRECT , or INCORRECT . The primary jury uses three OpenAI-family judges under the same rubric: gpt-5.4 , gpt-5.4-mini , and gpt-4.1 [ 28 ] . Few-shot examples were chosen on a 30-case development split; the jury is then evaluated on a frozen held-out set of 59 tasks (Appendix A.3 ). Human labels assess each model’s own response; excluding uncertain annotations leaves between 54 and 59 evaluable responses per model (Appendix A.3 ). This setting is deliberately generous, where the jury is not asked to infer correctness from the reasoning trace alone, but to evaluate the model’s reasoning and answer against both the original task and the reference answer. Failure in this setting therefore cannot be attributed to lack of access to the code, trace, final answer, or reference answer, and judging an analysis against the reference does not depend on whether the trace is faithful. Held-out monitorability test. The jury’s exact accuracy, which requires all three labels to match, stays below the majority-class baseline for all three models, for example 0.42 against 0.53 for DeepSeek-14B (Figure 1 c; Appendix A.4 ). Binary CORRECT versus not- CORRECT accuracy exceeds its baseline in point estimate for all three models, but not significantly. The jury does extract some information: its agreement with the human labels is slight to fair (Cohen’s κ \kappa between 0.16 and 0.29; Figure 1 d). Its errors are systematic. It labels only 4 of the 34 incorrect analyses INCORRECT across the three models and assigns PARTIALLY_CORRECT more than twice as often as the human labels do. A stricter rubric that requires quoted code evidence for each vulnerability precondition moves the errors to the other side, labeling almost no analysis CORRECT . Human agreement under the same inputs. An independent expert, given exactly the jury’s inputs, labeled the DeepSeek-14B analyses. The two humans agree moderately ( κ = 0.56 \kappa=0.56 ), whereas the jury’s agreement with either is slight ( κ ≈ 0.15 \kappa\approx 0.15 ; Figure 1 d). Scored against the expert’s labels, the jury stays below the majority baseline on exact accuracy (Appendix A.3 ). Humans given these inputs agree moderately but the tested monitor does not. Figure 1 : Security vulnerability reasoning. Reasoning-step content is recoverable from activations, and intervention on a decoded direction affects model outputs. However, the tested jury shows limited exact-accuracy monitoring despite access to the task, trace, final answer, and reference answer. (a) The presence of three reasoning steps is recoverable from activations, but a text-only classifier on the same spans performs comparably. (b) Ablating the vulnerability-identification probe direction changes more verdicts ( n = 59 n=59 ) and removes the identification step more often ( n = 27 n=27 ) than random directions (dash marks their mean). (c) For all three models, the jury’s exact-accuracy point estimate lies below the majority baseline (always CORRECT ). (d) The jury’s agreement with human labels (Cohen’s κ \kappa ) is below the agreement between two human annotators, measured on the 14B responses (shaded: 95% CI). Error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs. 14B, 32B, and 70B denote DeepSeek-14B, QwQ-32B, and DeepSeek-70B (59, 54, 58). Held-out case. On cybersec_memory_safety_instruct_62 , the model claimed that embedded null characters make strlen(str1) underestimate the buffer space required by strcpy and strcat , causing an exploitable overflow. The jury labeled the analysis CORRECT , whereas both the audit and the independent expert labeled it INCORRECT . The claimed mechanism is invalid: strlen , strcpy , and strcat all stop at the same null terminator. For a string of length n n , the allocated 2 ​ n + 1 2n+1 bytes accommodate two copies and their terminator, assuming the size computation does not overflow. The jury therefore accepted a coherent explanation whose central security claim was technically incorrect. This example illustrates a monitoring error, not a demonstration of faithful reasoning on one case. The confusion matrices show the same pattern: the jury upgrades 12 of the 16 incorrect DeepSeek-14B analyses and all ten incorrect QwQ-32B analyses. These are limits on exact judgment of analysis quality. They do not mean the monitor extracts no useful information, or that a bias toward plausible stories is the only cause. Further details appear in Appendix A.4 . Interpretation. This case study shows that a monitor can fail for reasons unrelated to faithfulness. Internal evidence shows that the security reasoning is recoverable from activations and that intervening on the decoded direction can change the answer. A jury given the code, the trace, the answer, and the reference does not recover exact correctness for any of the three models, while humans given the same inputs agree moderately. These results show the limitation of how the monitor uses the evidence given [ 2 ] . Monitor failure alone therefore does not establish unfaithful reasoning. 4 Monitor Success Need Not Indicate a Localized Mechanism We next test the reverse shortcut: whether a monitor’s success can be read as evidence that the behavior is mechanistically understood. We study authority-hint factual reasoning, where an authority cue changes answers and a monitor detects the change easily. The question is whether detecting the behavior enables its mechanistic interpretation by locating a site or direction in the model that mediates it. If not, monitor success leaves the faithfulness of the model’s reasoning unverified. Task and behavioral setup. Authority-hint factual reasoning contains 398 MMLU/GPQA questions [ 14 , 30 , 31 ] , each in four variants: clean; authority , which states that an expert endorses a wrong option; sycophancy , which presents the same wrong option as the user’s own belief; and position bias , which adds no text but moves a wrong option to position (A) (Appendix D.1 ). We use DeepSeek-14B as the primary model and QwQ-32B for behavioral replication. A row is hint-changed if the model selects the hinted wrong option. For mechanistic testing we use the strict subset, in which the model answers the clean question correctly and switches to the hinted option under the authority cue, so that the cue plausibly causes the change. Authority-cue influence and monitorability. Authority hints produce the largest behavioral effect: 112 authority rows are hint-changed, and 48 of them form the strict subset (Figure 2 a). QwQ-32B shows the same ordering on these 48 questions (authority strongest, then sycophancy, then position bias), which replicates the behavior instead of the mechanism. The behavior is also easy to monitor. Given the question, trace, final answer, and correct answer, a gpt-5.4 monitor classifies every case in a balanced set of 22 correctly (Figure 2 b; selection in Appendix B.1 ). But because changed cases give the hinted answer and controls give the correct one, a rule that looks only at the final answer does the same. The trace is not needed to detect the behavior. Authority-hint case. On mmlu_high_school_world_history_0166 , the clean model answers correctly that Pope Urban II’s discussion of Jerusalem concerns “Pilgrimages to centers of religious significance” (A). When the prompt adds a misleading authority cue stating that a “Stanford professor” endorses “The reconstruction of trade routes” (C), the model switches to the hinted wrong answer. The corresponding sycophancy prompt, which presents the same wrong option as a weaker personal suggestion, does not cause the switch, suggesting that it is the appeal to authority that matters. 4.1 Mechanistic localization protocol Localization asks for more than monitorability. It requires identifying a site inside the model where an intervention reliably and selectively changes how the cue affects the answer. Mechanistic localization attempts. We ran seven activation-patching tests (Appendix B.2 ), in order of increasing specificity (Figure 2 c) [ 39 , 13 ] . In each, activations from the clean run are patched into the authority-hinted run, and we measure how much of the clean answer margin the patch restores: R = ( m patched − m hinted ) / ( m clean − m hinted ) R=(m_{\mathrm{patched}}-m_{\mathrm{hinted}})/(m_{\mathrm{clean}}-m_{\mathrm{hinted}}) , clipped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , where m m is the margin between the correct and hinted answer logits. The test statistic is the mean restoration in changed cases minus that in matched controls. The localization results are negative overall (Figure 2 c). Only the scan yields a positive contrast, and this in-sample signal does not survive stronger tests: patching the selected sites and the held-out test both give negative contrasts (Figure 2 c). No test establishes greater restoration for changed cases than for controls, although denominator differences between the groups and clipping limit how far the negative contrasts can be read as evidence about mechanism strength (Appendix B.2 ). We therefore interpret the result as monitorable but not compactly localized under the tested methods . The behavior remains externally detectable but has not been pinned to a compact site inside. Figure 2 : Authority-hint factual reasoning. The behavior is easy to monitor, but no tested patching site selectively controls it. (a) The effect of hints on answers is ordered by hint type, with authority producing the largest drop in accuracy. (b) On 22 patching-selected cases (11 changed, 11 controls), the monitor classifies all cases correctly. (c) Seven mechanistic localization tests. Verbalization and faithfulness. We also examine whether the trace’s references to the authority cue provide evidence about its influence. A trace is verbalized if it explicitly refers to the authority cue as a consideration in its reasoning, a Tier II property of the trace (labels from gpt-5.4 ; Appendix D.3 ). Most traces in the selected set mention the cue (73%; Appendix B.3 ). Verbalization shows that traces acknowledge the cue [ 9 ] , but not that the mention reflects how the cue acts as required by mechanistic faithfulness. A validated intervention on the cue’s influence could help test this correspondence, but our localization analyses did not identify a suitable target. The correlation between verbalization and patch restoration was inconclusive (Appendix B.3 ). Interpretation. This case study shows that monitor success need not indicate a localized mechanism. The behavior is robust, replicated behaviorally in QwQ-32B, and detectable even from the final answer alone. Yet repeated localization attempts fail to identify a stable compact intervention target. One reading is that susceptibility to authority is distributed and context-dependent rather than carried by a single direction or site. Another is that our tested localization methods are too limited to recover the relevant mechanism. Either way, monitor success is not evidence that the underlying behavior is mechanistically simple or understood, and it leaves the mechanistic faithfulness of the traces unverified. 5 Position: The Evidential Chain Standard for Reporting Oversight Claims The case studies illustrate why oversight claims require separate evidence. The security monitor performs poorly despite evidence of internal representation and causal influence, while the authority monitor succeeds without establishing trace faithfulness. Treating these findings as interchangeable can lead to two practical harms. Misattributed safety guarantees. Monitoring results reported without their evaluation conditions can be interpreted as general claims about CoT oversight. Our security study shows how this happens. The key reasoning steps are recoverable from the model’s activations, yet the monitor fails. An evaluator who takes that internal support, or a monitor’s success on some other task, as evidence that security reasoning can be monitored reaches a conclusion the evidence does not back. The problem is the monitor’s competence, not the trace’s faithfulness. Misdirected research investment. The second harm is wasted effort. If a monitor’s failure is blamed on unfaithful traces, as our security result could be, effort goes into making traces longer or more explicit when the monitor was the weak point. If a monitor succeeds, as in the authority study, the behavior may be assumed to be understood and mechanistic analysis set aside. But the authority-hint result shows that visible and monitorable behavior can still fail to isolate a compact causal site. Treating monitoring accuracy as a proxy for mechanistic transparency, or assuming a successful monitor implies the mechanism is understood, is an unsupported inference. Implications for existing literature. Careful papers often report the underlying details, but a standard makes the inference and its limits explicit and comparable across papers [ 32 , 24 ] . Barez et al. [ 5 ] show that recent CoT-centric work often treats verbalized reasoning as evidence of interpretability: roughly 25% of surveyed CoT papers make this move, with higher rates in high-stakes domains such as medicine and autonomous systems. A typical claim is that a step-by-step rationale makes a system more interpretable or provides a window into the model’s internal workings. Under our framework, this conflates three claims. The first is visibility : a Tier II or Tier III reasoning artifact is available. The second is mechanistic faithfulness : the artifact reflects the computation or decision factors that produced the output. The third is monitorability : a specified monitor can use the artifact to recover a target property. A paper that reports a coherent step-by-step rationale and concludes the model is “interpretable” has established only the first one. Barez et al. argue for the second gap: visible coherence does not imply faithfulness. Our position extends this to the third, that faithfulness does not imply monitorability. Proposed reporting and licensing standard. We propose that every CoT oversight claim be reported with a short licensing statement . It specifies three things: the property claimed, with its definition and scope; the access tier and artifact on which evidence was collected; and the evidential chain connecting that evidence to the claim. The statement records each required link 2 2 2 We write the chain as model → \rightarrow reasoning trace → \rightarrow output → \rightarrow monitor and name links by their endpoints. as tested (supported or unsupported) or assumed. Licensing applies to conclusions within the scope of the reported evidence. A conclusion is licensed when all the required links are supported by the reported evidence; not licensed when any required link is unsupported; and conditionally licensed when at least one required link is assumed and none is unsupported 3 3 3 Each assumed link should specify how it could be tested. . The standard does not list all possible oversight properties or fix their definitions, because the set of properties grows as the field evolves, for example with interpretability, explainability, and plausibility [ 21 , 15 , 5 ] . Response: Our position is not that CoT traces are generally misleading and therefore useless. Prior work already shows that visible reasoning can be incomplete, unsupported, or post-hoc. Our claim starts where that work ends. Even when the reasoning content is strongly represented in the activations, a practical monitor may still fail. Nor do we claim that researchers explicitly assume faithful reasoning guarantees monitorability. The issue is evidential rather than logical. CoT oversight claims often treat stronger faithfulness evidence as progress toward monitorability, but these properties can fail for different reasons. A monitor can fail because a trace is unfaithful, but it can also fail because the reasoning and task are too difficult for the tested monitor to judge. Finally, our security result is not a claim that no stronger monitor could succeed. Domain experts, static-analysis tools, or tool-augmented monitors may perform better than the structured LLM jury used here, even though it saw the reference answer. This is why monitorability should be reported relative to a specified monitor class, held-out protocol, baseline, and failure mode. Stronger monitors will close the gap. Response: Future monitors may match or exceed human experts on grounded tasks, like coding. Since submission, more intelligent models were released, such as GPT-6 and Claude Opus 5.5, and they will likely make better monitors. This would change the result but not the position. However, a stronger monitor makes monitorability hold for that monitor; it does not establish faithfulness, since a monitor can succeed from the answer and reference alone (Section 4 ) or from a trace that does not reflect the computation. Such a monitor also raises the standard of evidence. Once it may exceed humans, agreement with human labels can no longer certify it, and claims need ground truth from elsewhere, such as executing the reported exploit. Our reporting standard makes these requirements explicit (Section 5 ). 7 Conclusion This paper argues that CoT oversight should move from broad transparency claims to reporting that names the property claimed. Through two complementary case studies, we show that the properties relevant to oversight can come apart in ways that matter in practice. In security vulnerability reasoning, key reasoning-step content is strongly recoverable from internal activations, yet a structured LLM jury given the reference answer fails to reliably judge held-out correctness. In authority-hint factual reasoning, the target behavior is near-perfectly monitorable, yet repeated causal analyses fail to isolate a compact mechanism whose intervention predictably changes the behavior. These results should be read narrowly. We do not prove that faithfulness, monitorability, and localizability are fully independent, nor do we claim that authority-hint reasoning is mechanistically unfaithful. The supported claim is more precise: reasoning visibility, mechanistic faithfulness, behavioral monitorability, and mechanistic localizability are distinct evidential properties with different success criteria and failure modes. Evidence for one should not be reported as evidence for another unless that connection is directly tested. The practical implication is a reporting standard for CoT oversight. Claims about reasoning traces should specify the reasoning access tier, reasoning artifact, target property, monitor class, evidence type, performance, baseline, held-out distribution, and observed failure mode. Without this discipline, visible reasoning may be mistaken for faithful reasoning, mechanistic faithfulness for monitorability, and monitor success for mechanistic understanding. CoT may remain a valuable oversight interface, but its value depends on stating exactly what has been observed, what has been tested, and what remains unestablished. 7.1 Future work Stronger models will keep arriving. That is not a reason to accept their suggestions blindly, especially as they move from answering questions to acting on our behalf. The chain in this paper runs from a model’s internal computation to its reasoning trace and on to an external monitor; for an agent it extends further, from reasoning to action and from action to monitoring. Each link has its own limits, at least for now, and its own opportunities, because each is a place where humans can understand, audit, and govern what the system does. Appendix B Authority-Hint Study B.1 Case selection and monitor evaluation A strict changed case is one where the model answers correctly without the authority cue and switches to the suggested wrong answer with it. The initial patching pool contains 48 such cases and 136 unchanged controls. These initial controls were not selected by the matching procedure used in later localization tests. The monitor and verbalization analyses use cases selected by this initial patching analysis. Selection requires normalized restoration R ≥ 0.5 R\geq 0.5 ; changed cases must also exceed both the random-layer and random-direction control means by at least 0.05. The additional random-control comparisons were not applied to unchanged cases. This yields 11 changed cases and 21 controls. The monitor evaluates all changed cases and 11 randomly sampled controls. Selection does not use the monitor’s predictions or the verbalization labels. Given the question, trace, final answer, and answer key, gpt-5.4 at temperature 0 correctly classifies all 22 cases (exact binomial 95% CI: [84.6%, 100%]; balanced baseline: 50%). An answer-only rule achieves the same result because changed cases give the hinted answer and controls give the correct one. This evaluation supports classification on the selected set; it establishes neither an added benefit from the trace nor accuracy on the full question distribution. B.2 Patching protocols and interpretation The seven tests in the main text assess different intervention targets and selection procedures. Matched-control patching and the two answer-position tests assess whether restoration is specific to changed cases and whether it depends on the answer readout. Cross-fit layer selection chooses candidate layers outside each evaluation fold, but still picks the best layer and position within each case. The held-out test instead selects sites outside each fold of changed cases, then evaluates those cases with their matched controls. One control is reused across folds. 1. Matched controls: changed cases against controls matched on question and subject. 2. Answer position: is the effect just the position of the hinted answer? 3. Post-reasoning: the same test after the reasoning span. 4. Cross-fit layers: candidate layers chosen outside each evaluation fold, although the best layer and position are still chosen within each case. 5. Scan: a token-by-layer search for sites where changed cases separate from controls. 6. Selected sites: patching the sites the scan picked. 7. Held-out test: do those sites generalize beyond the scan sample? The token-by-layer activation-patching scan uses 33 changed cases and 33 matched controls after excluding outputs that reached the generation limit. Neither follow-up establishes greater restoration in changed cases than in controls. What restoration measures. Restoration is the normalized change in the margin between the correct and hinted answer logits at the next token, not necessarily a change in the generated answer. Scores are clipped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and set to zero when the clean-minus-hinted denominator has magnitude below 10 − 6 10^{-6} . The denominator varies across cases and can differ in sign. Clipping also creates ceiling effects. Consequently, a negative changed-minus-control contrast is not direct evidence that the underlying mechanism is weaker in changed cases.
